summary: Defines an optional extension to the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP) called Connection Establishment for Media Anchoring (CEMA). It lets middleboxes anchor an MSRP connection without having to modify MSRP messages, which also allows secure end-to-end communication. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Two friends pass messages through a helper in the middle. This trick lets the helper hold the line open without opening or changing the messages, so they stay private.

questions: how do middleboxes anchor msrp connections
msrp end to end security through middleboxes
what is the sdp msrp-cema attribute
subtitle: How chat-style MSRP connections can pass through media-anchoring middleboxes without the middlebox opening the messages.

tldr.problem: MSRP messages carry routing information inside them, so a middlebox that anchors the connection by rewriting SDP addresses breaks MSRP unless it reads and rewrites the messages itself, which costs resources and exposes them in cleartext.
tldr.mechanism: CEMA adds an SDP attribute, msrp-cema, that tells the peer to open its TCP or TLS connection to the address in the SDP c/m-line instead of the MSRP URI in the path attribute, so a middlebox only has to rewrite the SDP address.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can keep TLS end to end through middleboxes. The extension is optional and falls back to RFC 4975 behavior when the other side or the middlebox does not cooperate.

today: RFC 6714 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2012 and the data shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: The Problem with MSRP and Middleboxes
sections.content:
The Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP, RFC 4975) expects to use MSRP relays (RFC 4976) for NAT traversal and policy enforcement. Many SIP networks that carry MSRP also contain middleboxes: devices that anchor and control media, handle NAT traversal, monitor performance, bridge address domains and enforce interconnect policy. The RFC gives the 3GPP Interconnection Border Control Function (IBCF) as one example.

Middleboxes anchor media by changing the address and port in the SDP c/m-line. MSRP cannot cope with that. An active endpoint opens its connection to the MSRP URI in the SDP path attribute, so the connection skips the middlebox unless the middlebox also rewrites that URI. If it does rewrite it, the URI comparison in RFC 4975, which needs the message addresses to match the path URI, fails.

The only workaround is for the middlebox to act as an MSRP B2BUA: it terminates the MSRP session and starts a new one toward the real peer. That takes substantially more resources and exposes every message in cleartext, which violates the end-to-end principle.
sections.eli5: Imagine a post office that insists on opening every letter just to change the address on the outside. It is slow, and everyone can read your mail.

sections.title: The CEMA Idea
sections.content:
Connection Establishment for Media Anchoring (CEMA) is an optional MSRP extension. Endpoints that support it use the address in the SDP c/m-line, not the MSRP URI in the path attribute, to open the TCP or TLS connection. A middlebox that wants to anchor the connection then does what it already does for other media types: it rewrites the c/m-line.

CEMA is backward compatible. A CEMA endpoint talking to a non-CEMA endpoint behaves like a plain RFC 4975 endpoint. CEMA only changes how address information for the connection is negotiated. Once the connection exists, the normal rules of RFC 4975 and, when a relay is used, RFC 4976 apply.

Support is signalled by the SDP msrp-cema attribute in the MSRP media description. The extension also depends on the alternative connection model of RFC 6135, which lets an endpoint choose to be active or passive using the SDP setup attribute, and CEMA endpoints MUST support it.
sections.eli5: Instead of reading the address written inside the letter, both friends agree to use the address on the envelope, which the helper is allowed to change.

sections.title: Offerer and Answerer Procedures
sections.content:
A CEMA offerer builds its SDP offer as RFC 4975 says, and then MUST add msrp-cema to the MSRP media description. Without a relay it MUST include a setup attribute. With a relay it puts the relay address both in the topmost path attribute and in the c/m-line, and MUST include setup:actpass.

The answerer checks the offer. If there is no msrp-cema attribute and the c/m-line does not match the path URI, the answerer assumes a non-CEMA middlebox changed the address without acting as a B2BUA. It MUST then reject the MSRP stream (zero port) or the whole request with a 488 Not Acceptable Here response.

Otherwise the answerer MUST include msrp-cema in its answer, with a setup attribute if it uses no relay, or setup:passive and the relay address in the c/m-line if it does. An endpoint that ends up active MUST connect to the c/m-line address. A passive endpoint waits for the connection.

If the answer lacks msrp-cema and the addresses do not match in a way that would break the connection, the offerer MUST fall back to RFC 4975 by sending a new offer without msrp-cema. In that case a middlebox is assumed to act as an MSRP B2BUA.
sections.eli5: Each side says "I know the new trick." If both do, they use it. If one side does not, they go back to the old, slower way.

sections.title: Fallback and Address Matching
sections.content:
CEMA is not enabled in several cases, and the endpoints then use RFC 4975 and RFC 4976 procedures. Examples are a non-CEMA endpoint that becomes active, a non-CEMA endpoint that uses a relay and becomes passive, and a CEMA endpoint that uses a relay and would have to be active. The answerer also falls back when both endpoints use relays.

To decide whether a c/m-line was rewritten, an endpoint compares it with the path MSRP URI. The IP address comes from the c-line and the port from the m-line. For the URI, both come from its authority part, which always has a port. A fully qualified domain name is resolved with DNS first. IPv6 addresses are converted to the same representation using RFC 5952 before comparing, and if DNS returns several records, at least one must match.

If the answerer uses a relay and its c/m-line matches one of its path attributes, the offerer assumes there is no middlebox and falls back without sending a new offer.
sections.eli5: To tell if the helper changed the address on the envelope, you compare it with the address inside. If they differ, someone in the middle touched it.

sections.title: What the Middlebox Must Do
sections.content:
The RFC does not standardize middlebox behavior, but it assumes some. The middlebox is MSRP aware: it acts as an MSRP B2BUA when the offerer does not support CEMA, and merely rewrites the c/m-line when the offer carries msrp-cema. If it acts as a B2BUA, it never forwards the msrp-cema attribute. If it does not do this, CEMA endpoints may be unable to interoperate with non-CEMA endpoints across it.

Because the middlebox does not parse MSRP payloads, it probably cannot reuse one TCP connection for several MSRP sessions. It often assigns a unique local address and port to each session, so two middleboxes may hold a separate connection per session. Without that, it might forward messages to the wrong destination.

The middlebox must also be able to modify the SDP. With end-to-end SDP integrity protection it cannot anchor media, because the signaling would fail. In the TLS case, a CEMA middlebox relays packets at the transport layer, so the TLS handshake can run peer to peer and the middlebox only sees encrypted data. Under RFC 4975 fallback it acts as a TLS B2BUA instead and can read and change the messages.
sections.eli5: The helper has to promise two things: change only the outside address when both friends know the trick, and give each pair of friends their own mailbox number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
CEMA lets middleboxes tunnel TLS so that endpoints keep end-to-end security associations. Without it, middleboxes would have to read and modify cleartext MSRP, making end-to-end confidentiality and integrity impossible. The RFC recommends TLS, notes that MSRP endpoints are required to support it, and warns that without TLS CEMA might make it easier for a man in the middle to insert itself and monitor traffic.

Two authentication styles apply. Name-based authentication uses certificates bound to a hostname or SIP address of record and does not depend on trusted signaling. Fingerprint-based authentication uses self-signed certificates with a fingerprint sent in SDP. It needs integrity-protected signaling, and since the SIP Identity mechanism (RFC 4474) may not work when middleboxes edit the SDP, clients must trust the whole signaling path. Any proxy could replace the fingerprint and insert a TLS B2BUA.

For fingerprints, endpoints SHOULD store fingerprints when first seen and SHOULD warn when a new one appears for a seemingly same peer. Signaling over the Internet SHOULD NOT be trusted, and if the network is not trusted, endpoints SHOULD NOT use fingerprint-based authentication. It is also RECOMMENDED that CEMA endpoints support self-signed certificates with the Certificate Management Service (RFC 6072).
sections.eli5: Sealing the envelope only helps if you know who you are really talking to. You either check an ID card or trust the people carrying the introduction.

sections.title: SDP Attribute Registration
sections.content: The msrp-cema attribute is a media-level SDP attribute that carries no value. Its ABNF is simply msrp-cema-attr = "msrp-cema", added as an attribute alternative to RFC 4566. IANA added it to the media-level attribute registry of the SDP Parameters registry. Its purpose is to show that the creator of the SDP supports the CEMA mechanism.
sections.eli5: It is a single secret word written on the note that says "I know the trick."
